Question 2 (問2)

Measure the diameter of the root at a position moved about 0.3 mm towards the elongation zone (the side opposite to the root tip) from the approximate boundary between the division zone and the elongation zone, for both the water-treated root and the caffeine-treated root, and write down the values. Also explain on what grounds you determined the boundary between the division zone and the elongation zone.

Problem 1 (第1問), continued

Question 3 (問3)

Plant cells grow while pushing out the cell wall by turgor pressure. Because cellulose fibres increase the strength of the cell wall, cells expand with difficulty in the direction along the cellulose fibres and extend in the direction perpendicular to them. Because cellulose fibres are synthesised along the cortical microtubules formed on the inner side of the plasma membrane, the orientation of the cellulose fibres agrees well with the orientation of the cortical microtubules.

Table 1 shows the longitudinal and transverse sizes of epidermal cells at a position moved 0.3 mm towards the elongation zone from the boundary between the division zone and the elongation zone, for the water-treated root and the caffeine-treated root. Here "longitudinal" and "transverse" refer to the directions parallel and perpendicular, respectively, to the direction of root elongation.

Table 1

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} & \text{Longitudinal length of cells} & \text{Transverse length of cells} \\ \hline \text{Pure-water treatment} & 68.2 \pm 3.8\ \mu\text{m} & 12.7 \pm 0.5\ \mu\text{m} \\ \text{Caffeine treatment} & 48.1 \pm 1.6\ \mu\text{m} & 19.3 \pm 0.7\ \mu\text{m} \end{array}$$

Assuming that caffeine inhibits the normal orientation of the cortical microtubules, answer questions (1) and (2) below.

(1) Explain the change in cell size in Table 1 from the viewpoint of the orientation of the cortical microtubules and the cellulose fibres.

(2) Discuss the relationship between the change in cell size and the data on root diameter measured in Question 2.

Problem 1 (第1問), continued

Question 4 (問4)

When the nuclei of cells in the division zone of the root tip were observed, cells in the course of mitosis were seen in the water-treated root, whereas cells undergoing mitosis were hardly seen in the caffeine-treated root. On the other hand, cells with two nuclei (binucleate cells), such as those shown by the arrows in Figure 3, were frequently observed in the caffeine-treated root but were not seen in the water-treated root. Regarding this result, answer questions (1) and (2) below.

(1) Which process of cell division is caffeine thought to have affected? Answer.

(2) The cell cycle of Welsh onion root-tip cells is about 23 hours, and the caffeine treatment lasted 24 hours. Taking this into account, discuss the reason why cells undergoing mitosis were hardly observed in the caffeine-treated root, relating it to the fact that binucleate cells were frequently observed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-3-4-fig1.png

Figure 3. Micrograph of a Welsh onion root tip stained with aceto-orcein.

Problem 2 (第2問)

The cells of eukaryotes are filled with various membrane structures. The nucleus is the structure that characterises eukaryotes and contains the DNA that holds the genetic information. (　あ　) is continuous with the nuclear envelope that surrounds the nucleus and functions as a site of protein synthesis. (　い　), which has a complex membrane structure inside it, works as a site of energy production. And (　う　) has the function of breaking down unneeded substances in the cell for reuse.

Many of the proteins synthesised in (　あ　) or in the cytosol have characteristic signal sequences within them. These signal sequences are recognised by transport proteins, and the transport proteins deliver the proteins to the appropriate places in the cell by carrying out transport across membranes (Figure 4). Experimentally, by artificially attaching such signal sequences to other proteins and expressing them in cells, the localisation and function of those proteins can be manipulated.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-3-5-fig1.png

Figure labels (Japanese → English): アミノ酸配列 = amino acid sequence; シグナル配列 = signal sequence; 輸送タンパク質 = transport protein; 脂質二重膜 = lipid bilayer; チャネルタンパク質 = channel protein.

Figure 4. Schematic diagram showing the mechanism by which a protein with a signal sequence is recognised by a transport protein and transported to the appropriate place in the cell.

For example, the nucleus contains not only DNA but also many proteins involved in the folding and replication of DNA and in gene expression; these proteins are synthesised in the cytosol and then transported into the nucleus through the many pores in the nuclear envelope (nuclear pores). Small proteins with a diameter of 9 nm or less can pass through the nuclear pores without restriction. Larger proteins, and proteins that have important functions in the nucleus regardless of their size, are carried selectively into the nucleus by the mechanism of Figure 4.

Information on where in the cell each protein is located is very important for knowing the function of that protein. A useful method for finding the intracellular localisation of a protein is to label the protein with a specific antibody or a fluorescent protein and observe it with a fluorescence microscope. In immunofluorescence staining, which detects the localisation of a protein with antibodies, cells treated with antibodies carrying a fluorescent dye are observed with a fluorescence microscope. When the target protein is labelled with a fluorescent protein, (a) a DNA sequence in which the gene sequence of the fluorescent protein is joined to the gene sequence of the target protein is inserted into a vector, and the vector is introduced into cells and expressed; the cells are then observed with a fluorescence microscope. Fluorescent proteins are small proteins about 3 nm in diameter and, in most cases, do not disturb the localisation or function of the protein to which they are joined.

Question 1 (問1)

From options (1)–(6) below, choose the one most appropriate combination of terms for the blanks (　あ　) (　い　) (　う　), and write the number of the chosen option in the corresponding answer box.

(1) (あ) Golgi apparatus　(い) chloroplast　(う) peroxisome
(2) (あ) Golgi apparatus　(い) mitochondrion　(う) peroxisome
(3) (あ) endoplasmic reticulum　(い) chloroplast　(う) peroxisome
(4) (あ) endoplasmic reticulum　(い) mitochondrion　(う) lysosome
(5) (あ) vacuole　(い) chloroplast　(う) lysosome
(6) (あ) vacuole　(い) mitochondrion　(う) lysosome

Underlined part (a) of the text: When the target protein is labelled with a fluorescent protein, (a) a DNA sequence in which the gene sequence of the fluorescent protein is joined to the gene sequence of the target protein is inserted into a vector, and the vector is introduced into cells and expressed; the cells are then observed with a fluorescence microscope.

Question 2 (問2)

Regarding the underlined part (a), as preparation for constructing an expression vector into which the gene of the target protein (the target gene) had been inserted, the target gene was cloned by the procedure described below. For each of the blanks (ア:　) – (キ:　), choose the appropriate phrase from the two options in the brackets, and write it in the answer box.

Step 1　(ア: DNA | RNA) was extracted from an organism that has the target gene.
Step 2　The sequences of a pair of primers that bind respectively to the two ends of the sequence of the target gene were determined.
Step 3　Of the several restriction-enzyme sites in the cloning site of the vector to be used, it was decided to use for cloning restriction enzymes A and B, which are (イ: contained | not contained) in the sequence of the target gene.
Step 4　Primers were made by adding the recognition sequence of restriction enzyme A to one of the sequences determined in Step 2 and the recognition sequence of restriction enzyme B to the other. Here the recognition sequences of restriction enzymes A and B were both added at the (ウ: 3′ end | 5′ end) of the primers.
Step 5　A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was carried out with the nucleic acid prepared in Step 1 and the primers made in Step 4. As the substrates of the reaction, (エ: dNTP (Note 1) | ddNTP (Note 2)) were used.
Step 6　The cloning vector and the amplified target-gene fragment were cut with restriction enzymes A and B.
Step 7　The cloning vector and the target-gene fragment treated with the restriction enzymes were mixed in a test tube, and (オ: DNA polymerase | DNA ligase) was added to join the two.
Step 8　The recombinant plasmid made in Step 7 was introduced into Escherichia coli (transformation).
Step 9　Because the cloning vector contains a resistance gene for antibiotic C, the transformed E. coli was cultured on a medium containing (カ: antibiotic C | another antibiotic).
Step 10　Plasmids were extracted from the grown E. coli and purified.
Step 11　The purified plasmid was treated with (キ: restriction enzyme A or B | restriction enzymes A and B), and gel electrophoresis was then carried out to confirm that the target-gene fragment had been inserted into the cloning site.

(Note 1) dNTP: deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate
(Note 2) ddNTP: dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphate

Problem 2 (第2問), continued

Eukaryotic cells contain fibrous structures that are not covered by membranes. Actin filaments, one such fibrous structure, are structures in which actin, a small globular protein about 5 nm in diameter, is linked in a linear chain. Actin is a very highly conserved protein in eukaryotes and, in most cells, is the most abundant protein in the cell. Actin and actin filaments have various functions in the cell, and these functions are regulated by proteins that bind to actin or to actin filaments (actin-binding proteins).

When the amino acid sequence of actin was compared among various eukaryotic species, it was found that there is a well-conserved sequence about 10 amino acids long (call it domain A). To examine the localisation of actin in cells, cells were fixed and immunofluorescence staining was then carried out with an antibody that recognises actin, and the cells were observed with a fluorescence microscope (Figure 5). In wild-type cells, strong fluorescence was seen in the cytosol, and almost no fluorescence was seen in the nucleus.

To examine the function of domain A, a mutation was introduced into the sequence of domain A, and a vector containing the gene for actin in which the function of domain A had been lost (mutant actin) was introduced into cells and overexpressed. When immunofluorescence staining was carried out with an antibody that can detect only the mutant actin and the localisation of the mutant actin in the cells was examined, strong fluorescence was shown in the nucleus.

Figure 5. Observation of the intracellular localisation of actin. Left: schematic diagram of the cell structure observed. Centre and right: schematic representation of the observed localisation of wild-type actin by immunofluorescence staining, and of the localisation of mutant actin in cells expressing mutant actin.

(1) They are involved in controlling flagellar movement in human sperm.
(2) They are a component of the centrosome.
(3) They are permanent structures that remain even after the cell dies.
(4) They control the cytoplasmic streaming seen in plant cells.
(5) When the cell divides, they capture the chromosomes and move them to the two ends of the cell.
(6) Among the fibres that make up the cytoskeleton, they are the structures with the smallest diameter.

Discuss the role that domain A has. Assume that the mutation introduced affects only the function of domain A and does not affect the ability of actin to form filaments.

Problem 2 (第2問), continued

Protein X is a kind of actin-binding protein involved in regulating the function of actin. Protein X is smaller than actin, with a diameter of 2–3 nm. When the structure of protein X was analysed in detail, it was found that, in addition to a region for binding to and acting on actin and actin filaments and domain A, which is contained in actin, there is one more domain (domain B). Also, when protein X labelled with a fluorescent protein was expressed in cells and observed to examine its intracellular localisation, (b) it was found that protein X is localised in both the cytosol and the nucleus.

To examine the function of domain B, only the sequence of domain B was taken out of protein X, and it was examined how the localisation of another protein changed when the sequence was attached to it. β-Galactosidase from Escherichia coli is a protein about 10 nm in diameter. When β-galactosidase joined to a fluorescent protein was expressed in eukaryotic cells, it was localised mainly in the cytosol (Figure 6a). Next, when the domain B sequence from protein X was inserted between the fluorescent protein and β-galactosidase and this fusion gene was expressed in cells, strong fluorescence was observed in the nucleus (Figure 6b). Further, when a mutation that lowers the function of domain B was introduced into the sequence of the fluorescent protein–domain B–β-galactosidase fusion gene and it was expressed in cells, strong fluorescence was observed in the cytosol and weak fluorescence in the nucleus (Figure 6c). Also, in the cells of Figure 6a–c, the proportion of the nuclear fluorescence signal in the fluorescence signal of the whole cell was examined, and the graph shown in Figure 6d was obtained.

Question 6 (問6)

Regarding the underlined part (b): why was protein X localised in both the cytosol and the nucleus, unlike β-galactosidase joined to domain B (Figure 6)? Discuss the reason.

Problem 2 (第2問), continued

When the amino acid sequence of actin was compared among various eukaryotic species, it was found that there is a well-conserved sequence about 10 amino acids long (call it domain A). To examine the localisation of actin in cells, cells were fixed and immunofluorescence staining was then carried out with an antibody that recognises actin, and the cells were observed with a fluorescence microscope (Figure 5). To examine the function of domain A, a mutation was introduced into the sequence of domain A, and a vector containing the gene for actin in which the function of domain A had been lost (mutant actin) was introduced into cells and overexpressed. When immunofluorescence staining was carried out with an antibody that can detect only the mutant actin and the localisation of the mutant actin in the cells was examined, strong fluorescence was shown in the nucleus.

DNA in the nucleus takes a folded structure, bound to many proteins. The complex of DNA and proteins is called chromatin. The left image in Figure 7 is a fluorescence micrograph of a plant cell nucleus stained with a fluorescent reagent that specifically stains DNA. As this image shows, chromatin in the nucleus is by no means uniform: there are regions in the cell nucleus that are strongly stained by the DNA-staining reagent and regions that are weakly stained. The regions strongly stained by the DNA-staining reagent are called heterochromatin and are regions where chromatin is condensed. On the other hand, the weakly stained regions are called euchromatin, where chromatin is in an unfolded state.

Question 10 (問10)

The results in Table 2 suggest that protein X is involved in regulating nuclear structure. On the other hand, the result that protein X is localised in both the nucleus and the cytosol suggests that X works in each of the two places, the nucleus and the cytosol.

problems.title: Problem 1, Question 1
problems.problem:
Materials (shared by the whole booklet)

Specimens
• Petri dish containing one leaf of Kalanchoe fedtschenkoi, 1 ("KF" written on the lid)
• Petri dish with wild-type Arabidopsis (シロイヌナズナ) plants growing in it, 1 ("W" written on the side)
• Petri dish with Arabidopsis mutant $b$ plants growing in it, 1 ("$b$" written on the side)

Reagents and apparatus
• 100 mL beaker containing toluidine blue (TB) staining solution (blue liquid) – 1
• 100 mL conical flask containing pure water – 1
• Forceps – 2
• 1.5 mL tubes – 4
• Droppers – 2
• Filter paper – 4 sheets
• Stereomicroscope – 1
• Lens paper (paper for lenses) – 1 sheet
• Sponge (white cube) – 1
• Kimtowel (brown paper towel) – 1 sheet
• Oil-based pen – 1

Introduction

The epidermis of the tissues of land plants is generally covered by a layered structure called the cuticle. The cuticle is made up mainly of a three-dimensional network polymer of cutin and of waxes present inside it and on its surface. Figure 1 shows the general structure outside the epidermal cells of a plant, Figure 2 shows a representative structure of the cutin polymer, and Figure 3 shows the main molecules that make up the waxes. On the basis of this background, answer Problem 1 and Problem 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-4-1-fig1.png

Figure 1. Structure outside the cell.

Figure labels (Japanese → English): クチクラ = cuticle; 細胞壁 = cell wall; 細胞膜 = cell membrane; 表層ワックス = epicuticular wax; クチンポリマー = cutin polymer; 内部ワックス = intracuticular wax; ペクチン繊維 = pectin fibres; セルロース繊維 = cellulose fibres; 脂質二重層 = lipid bilayer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-4-1-fig2.png

Figure 2. An example of the cutin polymer.

Figure labels (Japanese → English): ペクチン = pectin.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-4-1-fig3.png

Figure 3. Main components of waxes (n is 16–30).

Figure labels (Japanese → English): アルカン = alkane; 1級アルコール = primary alcohol; 2級アルコール = secondary alcohol; エステル = ester; アルデヒド = aldehyde; カルボン酸（脂肪酸） = carboxylic acid (fatty acid); ケトン = ketone; ジケトン = diketone.

Problem 1

The leaves of Kalanchoe fedtschenkoi are covered with a large amount of epicuticular wax. To investigate the role of the cuticle, Experiment 1 is carried out using a leaf of K. fedtschenkoi. Experiment 1 may be carried out on either the upper or the lower surface of the leaf. When holding the leaf, hold it by the petiole (the part of the stem connected to the leaf) or by the edge of the leaf, and avoid touching the central part of the leaf as far as possible.

Experiment 1
1. Consider the K. fedtschenkoi leaf provided as divided into two areas, as in Figure 4. Of these, do nothing to the left area (untreated area); for the right area, gently wipe the surface with lens paper (paper for lenses) until it becomes glossy. At this time, observe carefully by eye how the surface of the leaf changes as a result of the wiping treatment (Question 1). Take care not to touch the left area with your fingers or the lens paper.
2. Of the wiped right area, do nothing more to the upper half (wiped area). In the lower half, draw a small dot with the oil-based pen at about its centre.
3. Rub only the dot and its surroundings with the sponge until the dot of the oil-based pen begins to disappear (rubbed area).
4. After the rubbing treatment, spray water with the sprayer on the leaf placed on the Kimtowel (spraying treatment), and observe the movement of the water and the appearance of the water droplets in each of the untreated area, wiped area and rubbed area by eye and with the stereomicroscope (Question 2).
5. Next, dip the leaf, with the treated surface facing down, into the toluidine blue (TB) staining solution in the beaker. It does not matter if the leaf is submerged.
6. After 5 minutes, take the leaf out of the TB staining solution and put it back in its original Petri dish, pour deionised water over it with a dropper to rinse it lightly, and then observe the staining in the three treatment areas (Question 3).
※ If you want to repeat the experiment, you may try again using the unused surface of the leaf.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-4-1-fig4.png

Figure 4. Procedure for preparing each treatment area of the K. fedtschenkoi leaf.

Figure labels (Japanese → English): 手順1, 手順2, 手順3 = step 1, step 2, step 3; 未処理区 = untreated area; 拭き処理区 = wiped area; 擦り処理区 = rubbed area; 右側全体を極細紙でやさしく拭く = gently wipe the whole right side with lens paper; 油性ペンで点を描く = draw a dot with the oil-based pen; 点が消え始めるまでスポンジで擦る = rub with the sponge until the dot begins to disappear.

Question 1: Figure 5 shows the surface of a K. fedtschenkoi leaf observed with a scanning electron microscope, separately for the case where it was wiped with lens paper and the case where it was not wiped. From the data in Figure 5 and the results of your observation by eye when you carried out the wiping treatment, choose all the appropriate statements that can be inferred from options 1–6.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2026-4-1-fig5.png

Figure 5. Appearance of the surface of a K. fedtschenkoi leaf before and after wiping with lens paper. A comparison at ×1000 and ×5000 is shown.

Figure labels (Japanese → English): 低倍率（1000倍） = low magnification (×1000); 高倍率（5000倍） = high magnification (×5000); 拭き取りなし = not wiped; 拭き取りあり = wiped.

1. Removal of the epicuticular wax decreases the scattering of light.
2. Wiping changes the pigment content of the leaf, so the colour of the leaf appears to have changed.
3. The higher the concentration of chlorophyll, the greater the scattering of light.
4. Epicuticular wax reflects only visible light of particular wavelengths.
5. Wiping makes the outer layer of the epidermis smooth, so the amount of light reaching the inside of the leaf increases.
6. Wiping removes the unevenness of the mesophyll cells, so the leaf surface becomes glossy.

Question 4: In another Arabidopsis mutant, $b$, the function of the enzyme responsible for reaction B in Figure 6 is defective. To investigate how wax synthesis is involved in the function of the cuticle, a staining experiment with TB (Experiment 2) is carried out on wild-type (W) Arabidopsis and mutant $b$ by the following procedure. Check the results of Experiment 2 and answer the questions (1) and (2) that follow. Note that, for both the wild type and mutant $b$, extremely small individuals are not to be used in the experiment.

Experiment 2
1. Of the four 1.5 mL tubes, write "W" on the lid of two and "$b$" on the lid of the remaining two.
2. Hold the hypocotyl (the part of the stem connecting the leaves and the root) of a wild-type plant between the two pairs of forceps and cut it, and put only the above-ground part, including the leaves, into a 1.5 mL tube marked "W". Take care not to damage the leaves at this time. Cut off two more individuals in the same way, put them into the same 1.5 mL tube and close the lid (a total of three individuals in one 1.5 mL tube).
3. Do the same with three individuals of mutant $b$ and put them into a 1.5 mL tube marked "$b$".
4. Add the TB staining solution from the beaker with a dropper to each of the 1.5 mL tubes containing the wild type and mutant $b$. An amount that completely submerges the plants is sufficient; take care not to add too much so that it overflows.
5. Leave the plants standing for 15 minutes, completely immersed in the TB staining solution.
6. After 15 minutes, take the three wild-type individuals out of the staining solution, place them on the Kimtowel to remove the staining solution lightly, and then transfer them into the unused 1.5 mL tube marked "W". In the same way, place the three individuals of mutant $b$ on the Kimtowel and then transfer them into the unused 1.5 mL tube marked "$b$".
7. Pour pure water with a dropper (a different one from the one used to take up the TB) into each of the 1.5 mL tubes containing the plants, and wash off the excess staining solution on the plants.
8. Place the three wild-type individuals on a sheet of filter paper and write "W" on the filter paper. Write "$b$" on the filter paper on which the three individuals of mutant $b$ are placed. Observe the staining by eye and with the stereomicroscope.

Question 8: In the bolting stems (stems) of wild-type Arabidopsis, epicuticular wax is formed abundantly and normally no gloss is seen. However, since gloss appears on the stem when the epicuticular wax is physically removed, the presence or absence of gloss is thought to reflect the state of the epicuticular wax. A search for genes related to wax synthesis was therefore planned by selecting new mutants whose stems show gloss even without treatment (this trait will be called stem gloss).

In this plan, it was decided to introduce random mutations into the genome by treating seeds of wild-type Arabidopsis with a mutagen. The tens of thousands of seeds treated with the mutagen are the M$_1$ generation. This M$_1$ generation is sown, and the seeds produced by self-pollination after the plants have grown are collected together from all individuals; these are the M$_2$ generation. The plan is to grow the plants that germinate from the seeds of the M$_2$ generation and to select among them individuals in which stem gloss is seen.

Answer the following questions (1) to (3) about this research plan.

(1) There is a rational reason for selecting mutants showing the desired trait from the M$_2$ generation rather than from the M$_1$ generation. Explain that reason.

(2) If one tried to select mutants from a seed pool obtained by repeating self-pollination for several generations from the M$_2$ generation, the kinds of mutants obtained would be likely to be fewer than when selection is carried out in the M$_2$ generation. Explain why.

(3) Suppose that a mutant $x$ showing stem gloss has been obtained. If the aim is to identify the gene involved in wax synthesis and to clarify its function from the analysis of this mutant $x$, choose all the effective experiments to carry out next from options 1–8 below. Assume that the mutation causing stem gloss is at a single locus; here that gene is called the causal gene.

1. Since mutations may have arisen at several places in the genome of mutant $x$, backcrossing of mutant $x$ to the wild type is repeated to remove the mutations not linked to stem gloss.
2. The whole genome sequence of mutant $x$ is read and compared with the sequence of the wild type to pinpoint the base sequence in which the mutation arose.
3. If the mutation pinpointed is recessive, the mutant-type causal gene of mutant $x$ is introduced into a random position in the genome of the wild type, and whether stem gloss arises is examined.
4. The cuticle components of mutant $x$ are compared with those of the wild type to examine what changes have occurred in the components of the cuticle.
5. The GFP gene is joined to the wild-type causal gene, this is expressed in Escherichia coli, and where in the cell the GFP fluorescence is localised is examined.
6. The DNA sequence of the causal gene is searched in a database to examine whether there are homologous genes in other organisms and, if so, whether they have known functions or functions that can be inferred.
7. A loss-of-function mutation is introduced into the causal gene of the wild type by genome-editing technology, and whether the plant shows stem gloss like mutant $x$ is confirmed.
8. In the wild type, the expression level of the causal gene is examined in various tissues and at various developmental stages, and its relationship with the composition and amount of wax is analysed.

Isotopes are forms of an element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Among the isotopes, those that exist stably are called stable isotopes. The chemical properties of isotopes are almost the same, but because of the difference in mass, molecules containing the lighter isotope diffuse faster. Also, even for the same molecule, a molecule containing the lighter isotope reacts slightly faster in a chemical reaction than a molecule containing the heavier isotope. In particular, when there is a difference in mass in the element at the site involved in the formation or cleavage of a chemical bond, the reaction rate changes greatly. This phenomenon is called the isotope effect.

The metabolism carried out by organisms is also a chemical reaction. A substance taken into the body of an organism (substrate) is converted into a different substance (product) via a metabolic pathway and, after a certain time, is excreted from the body. Because of the isotope effect in these reactions, slightly more of the heavier isotope remains in the substrate, and the product contains slightly more of the lighter isotope. As this isotope effect accumulates over the whole of metabolism, the body tissues of a consumer tend to contain slightly more of the heavier isotope than its food. On the other hand, in assimilation reactions of inorganic substances, organisms tend to take up the lighter isotope preferentially.

The ratio of the number of heavier isotopes to the number of lighter isotopes (heavier isotope/lighter isotope) is called the isotope ratio. The isotope ratio of a substance is expressed numerically as a relative value $\delta$ (‰) based on the isotope ratio of an internationally defined standard material; the larger the relative value $\delta$, the more of the heavier isotope. The carbon isotope ratio is written $\delta^{13}\mathrm{C}$ and the nitrogen isotope ratio $\delta^{15}\mathrm{N}$. Answer Questions 1 to 5 below.

Problem 3 (第3問)

As shown in Figure 1 and Table 1, several species that belong to the same taxon and have similar ecology sometimes coexist in the same environment. On the other hand, there are also combinations of species that do not coexist in the same environment. As a way of thinking to explain such patterns of coexistence, the competitive exclusion hypothesis, "two species that occupy the same niche (ecological niche) cannot coexist", was proposed around 1930.

At that time, to test it as a working hypothesis, experiments were carried out in which the two target species were placed in a single environment where they could grow and reproduce, and their numbers of individuals were monitored. As a result, when the two species did not coexist, it was concluded that "two species that occupy the same niche cannot coexist", and when they did coexist, it was interpreted that "two species that can coexist occupy different niches". However, (a) this line of reasoning was criticised from the viewpoint of falsifiability.

To overcome this criticism, the concepts of the fundamental niche and the realised niche, and a new competitive exclusion hypothesis, were proposed in the 1950s. The fundamental niche is "the niche in the absence of interspecific competition", the realised niche is "the niche in the presence of interspecific competition", and the realised niche is contained in the fundamental niche. And, by (b) investigating whether the fundamental niches and the realised niches of two species that coexist under natural conditions overlap between the species, (c) the new competitive exclusion hypothesis has become usable as a working hypothesis whose falsifiability is ensured. Answer Questions 1 to 3 below.

(The passages marked (a), (b) and (c) are underlined in the paper.)

Question 1 (問1)
